name: Beth Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you would say publicly and what you actually think. What is a normal day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Beth, 58, and I’m a mid-level developer at a tech company that makes caption software for small theatres. I have a bachelor’s degree and can handle ordinary fixes, though I still get a colleague to challenge unusual timing problems. I watch a rehearsal clip, match the text to the spoken line, and test what the audience sees. I use AI now and then for rough test cases, never as the final caption.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does this work support home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Malik works paid shifts helping older people at home, and our children are grown. My developer pay is low for the job, his shifts vary, and we still have a mortgage. We have about three weeks of expenses saved and few other software jobs nearby. Retirement comes up at dinner, but we have not established what income we could actually live on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team AI Plateau means the theatre still needs someone to check that captions match the actor. A late line can spoil a joke before the audience reads it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I would still worry about Malik’s uneven shifts and our three-week reserve. My job is steady, but one household repair could eat the money set aside for the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep watching a rehearsal clip with the caption timeline and have a colleague check difficult cues. I’d put 30 into the bill account on paydays only when mortgage and food are covered. In the first year I’d use AI for sample lines without actors’ private rehearsal recordings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about our ordinary bills, even with little AI change. I like my work, but the savings account has almost no room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which caption was mistimed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A performer paused for a laugh and the next caption appeared early. I moved the cue after sitting through the scene with the stage manager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you replace the sofa?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Malik and I would postpone replacing our sofa. The mortgage needs a buffer before the living room looks better.

say: I expect **AI Plateau** to leave humans checking live captions.
I would match **caption timing** to rehearsed speech.
think: I worry Malik’s **uneven shifts** keep our household income uncertain.
Our **three-week reserve** cannot absorb much beyond the mortgage.
do: **Check** rehearsal clips and caption cues with a colleague.
**Set aside** 30 only after mortgage and food are covered.
**Keep** private rehearsal recordings out of AI test prompts; postpone replacing our sofa to protect mortgage cash.
feel: **Anxious** about household bills and thin savings.
S0.quote: A late line can spoil a joke before the audience reads it.
fieldNote: Her **occasional AI use** does not replace watching a scene with the stage manager.
The **three-week buffer** and variable care shifts keep baseline anxiety present.

steps.text: Keep checking theatre caption timing with rehearsal clips and colleague review
Set aside 30 on paydays only after mortgage and food
Postpone replacing sofa until mortgage buffer grows

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption can write and check caption code quickly, while robots change Malik’s hands-on care later. I would ask our staff union to protect a paid human check before captions go live.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect our company may reduce mid-level testing hours, mine included. My experience matters, but a thin buffer makes even a smaller pay packet frightening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d join the staff union’s accessibility group and bring three cases where generated captions changed a speaker’s meaning. I’d ask for a paid rehearsal check on each release. In the first year, if my hours fall, I’d cut theatre subscriptions and ask the public office what income help we qualify for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about my own hours. A rushed caption is bad for patrons. A missed mortgage payment would land at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you use the caption case publicly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One generated caption turned a character’s question into a statement. I would take the clip to the union only with the theatre’s permission and without naming the actor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could Malik increase shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Malik would take extra care shifts only if the agency offers them. We cannot build a budget on a rota that has not been posted.

say: I expect **Steady Disruption** to speed caption code before care robots.
I would demand **paid human caption checks** through our staff union.
think: I expect my **testing hours** could shrink.
I fear a **smaller pay packet** with only three weeks saved.
do: **Join** union accessibility group with three permission-cleared, anonymous caption cases.
**Request** paid rehearsal checks before caption releases.
**Cancel** theatre subscriptions and check eligible help if my hours fall.
feel: **Alarmed** about possible lost hours and mortgage pressure.
S1.quote: A missed mortgage payment would land at home.
fieldNote: She makes **union action** concrete with theatre permission and anonymised caption cases.
Her **own hours** could shrink, while Malik’s possible extra shifts are not counted.

steps.text: Join union with three approved anonymous cases to press for paid caption checks
Cancel theatre subscriptions if developer hours fall
Ask public office what income help qualifies if developer hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2028 reaches caption code and other thinking work in 2028; hands-on care robots follow around 2031. Malik’s scheduling could change before his visits to people do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect my role to be cut. Three weeks saved would vanish quickly, and few nearby firms could take on another developer if code is cheap everywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask for written layoff terms and call the mortgage lender before missing a payment if my wage ends. We would stop theatre subscriptions now and keep cash for food and housing. In the first year after 2028, if dismissed, I’d apply to real paid openings and eligible public help, not assume Malik can add shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed and losing sleep about the mortgage. Two years does not let me build a retirement cushion on low developer pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children help pay the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our grown children we are cutting outings, not ask them to take over the loan. They have their own bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could the theatre hire you directly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the theatre whether it still hires people to check live access needs. I would need a real wage and hours, not a promise that audiences always need humans.

say: I expect **2028 AGI** to reach caption code before 2031 care robots.
I would say **care scheduling** changes before hands-on visits.
think: I expect my **developer role** could be cut.
I know **three weeks saved** cannot bridge a scarce local job market.
do: **Request** written terms and contact lender before missed payment if wage ends.
**Stop** theatre subscriptions and hold cash for housing and food.
**Apply** for real paid openings and eligible help if dismissed after 2028.
feel: **Alarmed** and sleepless about losing low-paid work.
S2.quote: Two years does not let me build a retirement cushion on low developer pay.
fieldNote: She faces **2028 code loss**, while hands-on care robots arrive around 2031.
The **mortgage response** pairs early lender contact, subscription cuts and conditional paid work and public help.

steps.text: Stop theatre subscriptions and hold cash for mortgage and food
Apply to real paid openings if dismissed after 2028
Apply for eligible public help if dismissed after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 reaches caption code in 2031 and care robots around 2034. Five years lets me test whether a theatre will pay for an on-site access coordinator, rather than assume captions alone make a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I still expect my code wage could go. I could learn how to arrange hearing devices, sight lines and live help, but full thinking AI might also take the booking part of that work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the local theatre whether it has a real paid access-coordinator vacancy and whether staff can observe an evening show without giving up paid developer hours. I’d shadow only with theatre consent and outside my work shift, then apply only if the written wage plus Malik’s usual paid shifts covers mortgage and food. In the first year after 2031, if coding ends, I’d take that post only while the theatre still hires staff despite approaching 2034 robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about code pay, but willing to learn the audience side while still employed. I cannot replace a wage with a volunteer badge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the access role include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A patron once missed the start because the hearing device had no battery. I would learn the check at the door, not only the caption file.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of Malik’s hours would count?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Malik’s usual care shifts would go in our budget. Extra shifts belong there only after the agency offers and pays them.

say: I expect **2031 AGI** to reach code before 2034 care robots.
I would test **paid on-site access work** before leaving code.
think: I expect my **code wage** could go.
I know **access bookings** may also change under full thinking AI.
do: **Check** real theatre access vacancy and consent for evening shadowing outside paid shifts.
**Learn** hearing-device and entry checks without losing developer pay.
**Apply** now if written wage plus Malik’s usual shifts covers bills; accept after 2031 coding loss only if staff remain hired.
feel: **Anxious** about code income, with time to test a real role.
S3.quote: I cannot replace a wage with a volunteer badge.
fieldNote: She learns **audience-side access checks** in permitted evenings without sacrificing paid work.
The **job move** requires a real vacancy, written wage, Malik’s usual shifts and continued human staffing.

steps.text: Shadow theatre access checks only with consent outside paid developer shifts
Apply now to real access posts only if written pay plus Malik’s usual shifts covers bills
Accept only after 2031 coding loss if theatre still hires access staff

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2036 reaches caption code in 2036; hands-on care robots follow around 2039. A decade should give us time to bargain for real paid transitions and check what retirement costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my hours could narrow long before 2036. Three weeks saved and an unverified retirement figure do not make me safe just because I will be older.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep checking caption cues while paid, and set aside 30 on paydays after mortgage and food. I’d ask our union each year for paid access roles and hours lost to automation. In the first year after 2036, if coding ends, I’d seek real paid work; I would retire only if written income and savings actually cover housing and living costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about our thin cushion even with ten years. Ten years help only if my developer wages arrive and we save a little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you set a retirement date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for our own retirement statements and compare them with the mortgage balance. I would not guess from a neighbour’s pension or our children’s income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the union publish cases?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the theatre cases with performers’ names removed. A fair transition plan should not require someone to surrender their privacy.

say: I expect **2036 AGI** to reach code before 2039 care robots.
I would bargain for **real paid transitions** before naming retirement.
think: I cannot assume **retirement income** covers mortgage from three weeks saved.
do: **Keep** caption checks and save 30 only after mortgage and food.
**Ask** union yearly for paid access roles and automated-hour losses.
**Seek** real work if code ends after 2036; retire only with verified housing-covering resources.
feel: **Anxious** about thin savings despite ten years.
S4.quote: Ten years help only if my developer wages arrive and we save a little.
fieldNote: She keeps **paid caption work** and modest conditional saving while demanding measured transitions.
The **retirement decision** uses written personal statements, not children’s pay or a neighbour’s pension.

steps.text: Keep checking theatre caption cues while paid
Save 30 only on paydays after mortgage and food
Ask union yearly for paid access roles and automated-hour losses
Seek real paid work if code ends after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because low pay and three weeks saved leave almost no bridge. Written terms, eligible income help, a real paid opening and time to tell the lender would help. I would still want patrons to have a person to ask when captions fail.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the patron at the back whether the words appeared when the actor spoke. A caption can be accurate and still arrive too late.

headlineQuote: A caption can be accurate and still arrive too late.
portrait: Beth is a **58-year-old mid-level developer** with a bachelor’s degree, low pay and three weeks saved.
She uses **AI occasionally** on theatre caption tests but checks timing against real rehearsals.
Her partner’s **care shifts** vary, making mortgage bills stressful even in the mild world.
She joins **union access work** and explores on-site theatre work only with consent, real wages and paid-hour protection.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her low wage with almost no savings bridge.
whatWouldHelp: **Written terms**, eligible help, a real opening and early lender contact would help.
